newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-INRO hopes to honour deadline on rubber pact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-INRO hopes to honour deadline on rubber pact.

text.p: The International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO) said on Friday it hoped to honour a year-end deadline for a new price pact although top producers Malaysia and Indonesia have not ratified the agreement.

INRO concluded the last council meeting of rubber producers and consumers on Friday and issued a statement expressing optimism that the International Natural Rubber Agreement 3 (INRA 3) could be ratified by all parties before the end of 1996.

But Malaysia and Indonesia, which have demanded that their representatives fill the executive director's post in INRO in exchange for ratifying INRA 3, left the meeting in deadlock, said officials who attended the talks.
The two countries together with Thailand account for nearly 90 percent of rubber production and without their ratification, INRA 3 cannot take effect, the officials said.
"Talks are still going on in regards to the issue," Zuber Ahmad, head of the Malaysian delegation to the council meeting, told Reuters. He declined to elaborate.

"The (Malaysia-Indonesia) issue was not officially raised at the council meeting," said James Hegarty, the buffer stock manager of INRO. "I don't know what their positions are, except that the council is on the whole optimistic about the INRA 3."

INRA 3, scheduled to come into force on January 1, 1997, will be the only remaining global commodity pact with economic provisions and a buffer stock that allows the industry to buy and sell rubber to stabilise prices.

Two cycles of the agreement -- INRA 1 and INRA 2 -- have been completed, but the third has been held over for a year due to delays in getting at least 75 percent of rubber producers and importers to sign and ratify the plan.
Malaysia's Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik warned recently that his government may not ratify INRA 3 if it is not granted the executive director's post in INRO.
The executive director's chair is the top post in INRO, the nucleus and administrative body of INRA. The post is now held by Thailand, which has already signed INRA 3.

Lim said Malaysia wanted the job because Thailand and Indonesia have had their representatives in the post under earlier agreements. But Indonesia argues that Malaysia already hosts the INRO headquarters in Kuala Lumpur and as such, the job should return to Jakarta.

Hegarty of INRO said on Friday that Austria was the latest to sign the pact, after the European Union decided that its members should provisionally implement INRA 3. The EU's support, following that of the United States and Japan, meant that 77 percent of rubber importers have agreed to apply the agreement.
